posts.author: elonmusk
posts.text:
India needs @Starlink 🇮🇳

• 11,256 of India’s listed villages still lacked 4G coverage as of May 2026.

• India had 1.093 billion internet subscriptions in March 2026, but only 440.87 million were rural. Rural subscription density was 48.31 per 100 people, compared with 126.80 in urban India.

• BharatNet had laid over 850,000 route-km of fibre and made about 221,000 Gram Panchayats service-ready. However, its Points of Presence were reported operational at only 80,472 Gram Panchayats in June 2026.

• Only 4.26% of India’s internet subscriptions were wired connections in March 2026. Starlink could give underserved communities another route to high-speed broadband.

• Starlink has already built 20 gateway sites in India, according to SpaceX Vice President of Starlink Business Operations Lauren Dreyer, speaking at India Mobile Congress today.

• Starlink says it has developed India-specific security controls designed to keep Indian user data within India.

• Its satellite network could bring high-speed internet to remote villages, mountains and islands where extending fibre or mobile networks is difficult.

• Better connectivity could help rural schools access online learning, clinics offer remote consultations and small businesses reach more customers. Starlink already supports education and healthcare in remote communities internationally.

• Portable Starlink terminals have supported disaster response around the world. They could give Indian emergency teams backup connectivity when floods, earthquakes or storms damage ground networks.

• Direct to Cell could also help ordinary 4G phones connect beyond tower coverage, subject to Indian approvals and mobile operator partnerships.

• The government itself identifies difficult terrain, low commercial viability and infrastructure constraints as reasons for remaining coverage gaps. This is exactly where Starlink could help India reach more people.

• India should complete the remaining clearances and spectrum allocation so Starlink can begin commercial service.

• SpaceX’s Vice President of Starlink Business Operations, Lauren Dreyer, said that Starlink is ready to help achieve Prime Minister Modi’s vision of 100% connectivity across India. She highlighted its potential to connect remote classrooms, support telemedicine and restore connectivity after disasters, adding, “With Starlink, people can get connected within minutes, not years.”

India’s hardest-to-reach communities deserve reliable internet too.

Finally I got tired of looking at them so I voice noted my lovely anthropomorphic assistant, Rose, to go through my messages on every social platform, texts, and email, compile the list, reach out to confirm addresses, find the best way to ship, and hand it all to my house manager.

One prompt. And she did it. No getting stuck, no random ass approval messages. It’s just handled. 

Some of you might say this has been possible for a while. You’re partially right, but it’s the frictionless experience that is the real game changer. If I have to keep pausing and explaining, or correcting mistakes, I’ll get frustrated and revert to procrastination.

posts.text:
In April 2009, Elon Musk was asked why General Motors wouldn't just buy Tesla. 

"You can't afford it." 

Fifty-five days later, GM was bankrupt.

He was 37, and his salary was $1.

In late 2007 his own car cost $140,000 to build. Tesla was selling it for $92,000, a $48,000 hole in every car, with the money almost gone.

November 2008: GM's Rick Wagoner flew to Washington on a $36 million corporate jet to ask Congress for $10 to 12 billion. A congressman asked him if he would work for $1 a year. Wagoner, paid $15.7 million in 2007, said he had no position on that today.

The clip is two moments from one evening at Silicon Valley's Churchill Club. In the first, Musk admits how close Tesla came to running out of money. In the second, he explains Detroit.

"Tesla was in a really dire situation at the end of 2007."

"This was inevitable. It was only a question of when."

That is Musk on April 7, 2009, four weeks after the stock market hit its crisis low and fourteen months before Tesla went public at $17 a share.

The money rules in that talk fit on an index card.

Know your floor before you need it. At 17, with a few thousand dollars, he tested whether he could live on under $1 a day, hot dogs and oranges bought in bulk.

Set the first target at groceries. Zip2 was started to cover food. It sold for over $300 million.

Learn the money side, or someone else decides for you. That is why a physics student also took an economics degree at Wharton.

If rent eats the business, cut the rent. He and his brother slept on futons in the office and showered at the YMCA.

Know your unit cost before you scale. That $48,000 hole nearly ended Tesla.

GM's bill went to the public: a $49.5 billion rescue, and $11.2 billion of it never came back to taxpayers.

In the same talk Musk said he would love to take over NUMMI, the GM and Toyota plant in Fremont, but couldn't afford it unless someone gave it to him. GM walked away from the plant in bankruptcy. Tesla bought it the next year for $42 million.

The full 93-minute talk is free on YouTube. In 17 years it has gathered about 333,000 views.

GM had billions of public money and still walked away from the factory. Musk started with one number: how little he could live on. Work out yours before you quit a paycheck.

Ballmer came to his house later that night to apologize. Gates did not.

Allen left Microsoft shortly after, but he kept all of his shares.

He was 30, cancer-free, and still owned nearly a third of the company. When Microsoft went public, that stake made him one of the richest people on Earth.

At one point, Allen was worth an estimated $40 billion.

Could you ever trust your co-founder again after hearing that conversation?
